newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Monitors dispute fairness of Zambia elections.
newsitem.headline: Monitors dispute fairness of Zambia elections.

text.p: A Zambian watchdog group said on Wednesday that this week's elections were effectively rigged, but a group of international monitors found the poll generally free and fair.

Monday's voting in presidential and parliamentary polls went ahead without "Father of the Nation" and former president Kenneth Kaunda, who led an opposition boycott of the campaign and called for economic sanctions on Zambia.

The Committee for a Clean Campaign, an umbrella group of 19 non-governmental and civic organisations which monitored the ballot, said that while the voting itself had been correct, the run-up to the elections was designed to give the ruling party an unfair advantage.

The committee said in a statement that flawed voter registration, abuses of government resources and partisan state-run media had favoured President Frederick Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD).
Half of Zambia's 4.6 million eligible voters were excluded from the rolls because of flawed registration.
"In view of all this, the 1996 presidential and parliamentary elections cannot be said to have been free and fair," the statement said.
An international observer group, however, said the election was "generally free and fair".
"The process was good and transparent, and we have not detected any evidence of foul play," said a statement by the monitoring group, working under the auspices of the Christian Council of Zambia.

"We did not see any evidence of rigging or intimidation," the international group added. It included monitors from a number of southern African states plus Canada, Denmark, Sweden, Australia and Germany.
Vice-President Godfrey Miyanda said the allegations of rigging were "unfortunate".
"The results must be accepted because that is what the people want. The question of rigging should not arise.
"If the election monitors are fair in their assessment, they will say the elections were free and fair," he told state radio.
Chiluba and his party were headed for a landslide victory in the polls, which took place on Monday. The MMD had won 82 of 96 parliamentary seats in which results had been announced.
Most opposition parties, including Kaunda's United National Independence Party, boycotted the voting and have said they will not recognise the results.
UNIP and the other main opposition grouping, the Zambia Democratic Congress, accused Chiluba of rigging the polls.
Both parties say they will rally their supporters against the results, and Kaunda was expected to follow up on his threat to step up a civil disobedience campaign.
Counting officials expected to have the final tally by late Wednesday.
The opposition boycott was sparked by the government's decision to effectively bar some candidates, including Kaunda, from challenging for the presidency.
Donor nations have frozen vital aid to Zambia this year, hoping to repeal the bar on Kaunda.

Chiluba, who took power from Kaunda in Zambia's first multi-party polls in 1991, rejected a public call from South African President Nelson Mandela to delay the election, saying this would be legally impossible.
